Your reasons are fairness, cost and prudence, and each covers one exit; my framing is that what all three share is that the rejection, if it was coming, never gets to arrive from another person, so you are never the one who was let go. insights.headline: You speak in the shop's second-person rule-voice at every choice point, and the rule form lets you act without ever having wanted anything; the one aborted "I didn't want to" in E3 is swapped for a rule mid-sentence.
insights.explanation: The register you learned from the one man who shaped you was second-person law: "you're holding the mic wrong," "you let the ratchet do it." You use it on yourself at each contestable decision: "you swept and you kept your mouth shut" (E1), "if you're gonna do it you do it" (E2), "the box you gotta take the drawers out" (E3), "you sign the thing that says it's your own lookout" (E4), "you leave a box dirty and that's what they remember" (E5), five of five. A rule cannot be refused or argued with; a want can. My framing: the grammar ensures no preference of yours ever appears in the record, so nothing you wanted can be denied. First person is for physical acts (I went, I ran, I took, I left); the switch to generic "you" lands on the decision or the exposure, not on the action.

insights.headline: Your body is nobody's business including your own: you act when a mechanical threshold is crossed and disclose to no one, so nobody is ever put in the position of tending you.

E4: you drive yourself in, tell no one at the shop, tell Nick seven months later only after Nick mentions his own blood pressure, and quit a medication without a call. E5: retired six months, and the only sentence about your days is "Then I don't know." Three of five stories carry health content, and in all three the self is withheld. Your stated reasons (vacation on the books, it came up, meant to call) explain each omission singly; my framing is that the silence across all of them forecloses anyone having to look after you, a position you have not once occupied in five stories. E4 gives the truck's mileage, model year, battery brand and warranty; the medications are "the one pill" and "the other one." Precision follows what you maintain yourself.

insights.headline: Your theory of legacy names only condition (a clean box, a name on the traveler), yet your own memory of Walt holds a gesture alongside a dead-on mic, and you grade your life "Not much of one" by the narrower standard.

You finish, clean and vanish, and pay for it each time in presence. But what you actually remember of Walt is not the mic's condition, it is a man setting a part down without meanness; your theory of what people remember is contradicted by the one memory you cannot stop turning over. My framing: that gap is why the summary of your life is "Not much of one"; you judge by story and only ever deposited condition. The objects you left behind are counted (three hundred dollars, drawers wiped); the people you left the room on are not described, and the verdict on your own story arrives in the same flat register as the closing dates elsewhere.

facts.what_happened: Speaker's first shop job was at a shop off East 12th near where the tracks cross.
The building no longer exists; the site is now a gravel lot used for trailers.
The year was 1983.
The speaker was eighteen years old.
The shop produced mostly hydraulic fittings and some valve bodies for a company in Cleveland.
An older man named Walt Zimmer worked at the shop.
Walt Zimmer operated the two Monarch lathes at the end; nobody else used them.
The speaker's job was sweeping.
The speaker's duties were sweeping and deburring.
Walt did not speak to the speaker for approximately four months.

Walt demonstrated the correct way to hold the micrometer.

Walt had a lung condition.
The lung condition was attributed to coolant mist; workers did not wear protective equipment at that time.
Walt left work around September and had died by Thanksgiving.
Walt's wife brought a box of his belongings to the shop and told the workers to take what they wanted; the workers stood there.
The speaker took the micrometer from the box.
The micrometer is a Starrett 436, one inch, carbide faces, with the initials W.E.Z. scratched in the frame with a vibro pen.
The speaker still has the micrometer.
It is kept in the second drawer of the top toolbox.
About two years ago the speaker checked it against gage blocks; it read accurately with no detectable anvil wear.
The speaker has had the micrometer for over forty years.
There is a headstone at Trinity with lettering; someone took care of it.
The speaker guesses the union local or someone else arranged the headstone.
The shop closed in 1987.

candidates.headline: He believes that if he can perform an ordinary act, he is well, and that a medical opinion contradicting that is a charge on an invoice rather than information.

facts.what_happened: Speaker has been retired since March 2026.
Before retirement there was talk at the plant.
The plant manager was walking around with an unfamiliar man who carried a tablet.
On a Monday the speaker went to HR and took the package before a list was issued.
Two weeks later a list came out with fourteen names on it.
Speaker does not know whether he was on the list.
His last day was a Thursday.
He arrived at six, emptied his toolbox, and wiped the drawers with a rag.
He took the Starrett, a dial indicator, a 0-1 test indicator with swivel, and his own tap wrenches.
He left the remaining tools.
About three hundred dollars of his own tooling remains in the shop.
A card was circulating and a cake was planned for two o'clock.
He left at 11:40.
He exited by the side door near the compressor room, put the box in his truck, and left.
He worked forty-one years total including a fittings place; thirty-four at this shop.
A worker named Devon, aged about 23-24, is at the shop.
Devon's micrometer set was Chinese-made; the ratchet on the two-inch gave four different readings.
Speaker bought a used Mitutoyo micrometer set from a man in Girard for $190, put it in Devon's drawer, and told Devon the company had them in the crib from the layoff.
Devon does not know the true source.
Devon uses the set.
Speaker now gets up at the same time as before.
He goes to the Denny's on Peach or the one near I-90.
He built a fly rod for Nick.
Six-weight fly rod, cork grip he turned himself, green wraps matching Nick's childhood hockey colors (Cascade green).
Rod was finished in June.
Rod is in a tube in the spare room closet.
Nick is visiting at Christmas.

candidates.headline: He speaks in Walt's rule-voice at every choice point, and the rule form lets him act without ever having wanted anything.
